title: Arjuna's austerities
hook: Arjuna fights the hunter with everything he has and loses, then lays a garland before Shiva and sees it on the hunter's head

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna's austerities brought him face to face with a hunter, and he picked a fight. Did you give someone one breath before deciding who they were? Day seven hundred eighty-five.

Everything Arjuna has, he throws at the hunter. This is the great archer, carrying the bow Gandiva and quivers the epic describes as never running out. He looses a storm of arrows. And the hunter simply stands there and takes them, unhurt, the way a mountain takes rain. Arjuna shoots and shoots, and then something happens he didn't expect. He reaches back, and the quiver is empty. Today, the fight Arjuna loses, and what he does next.
screen: `A STORM OF ARROWS.` → `THE HUNTER STANDS UNHURT.` → `THE QUIVER IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: So Arjuna fights with whatever is left. He strikes with the end of his bow, and the hunter snatches the bow away. He draws his sword and brings it down on the hunter's head, and the sword breaks. He fights with his fists. The two of them wrestle, and the hunter presses him so hard that Arjuna can't breathe, and he falls senseless to the ground. Everything his austerities built, the strength, the focus, the warrior's pride, has failed. And then, coming to, bruised and beaten, Arjuna does the thing he came to the mountain for in the first place. He stops fighting and turns to worship. He shapes an altar from earth, honors Shiva upon it, and lays a garland of flowers there. And when he looks up, he sees the garland. It's on the hunter's head. That's the moment of recognition. The flowers he offered to Shiva have arrived on the stranger he was trying to beat. Arjuna understands who has been standing in front of him all along, and he falls at Shiva's feet and asks forgiveness. And Shiva is pleased with him. Arjuna didn't win; in the telling, it's his courage in the fight that Shiva praises. Arjuna's austerities, it turns out, needed this last part. Fasting on air made him strong. Losing made him see. The god he was straining toward was right there, in a hunter he'd dismissed, and his own offering is what showed him.
screen: `THE BOW TAKEN, THE SWORD BROKEN.` · `ARJUNA FALLS SENSELESS.` · `A GARLAND LAID BEFORE SHIVA.` · then, large: `THE GARLAND ON THE HUNTER'S HEAD.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and loosen anything you're holding: the jaw, the hands, the shoulders. Bring to mind something you've been fighting hard. A problem, a person, a part of yourself. Breathe in, and feel how tired the fight has made you. Breathe out, and set it down for a moment, the way Arjuna set down his weapons and picked up flowers. You don't have to give up. Just stop pushing for these few breaths. If you pray, you can offer that struggle in your prayer. If not, simply rest. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna's austerities. They end in a lost fight, an altar of earth, and a garland found on the head of the hunter who was Shiva.
Your line: stop pushing, offer something instead. Today, in one struggle, try a different move: stop pushing for a moment, and offer something instead. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva retell Arjuna's defeat and recognition as a story of the god meeting his worshipper in disguise, and the garland found on the hunter's head is a remembered detail of the story.

myth: Arjuna defeated the hunter and then learned he was Shiva

he laid it on an earthen altar to Shiva and then saw it on the hunter's head.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. your arrows are gone, your sword is broken, and you've just woken up on the ground. what do you do?
options: get up and fight again with your bare hands.
make an altar and worship Shiva.
fork.reveal: he worships Shiva with a garland, and then sees that garland on the hunter's head.

trapdoor: what you thought: Arjuna lost a fight to a stronger man.
what it means: the hunter was Shiva, and Arjuna's defeat led him to worship and to recognition.
what a scholar hears: the garland moves from the altar to the hunter, so the offering itself reveals who the god is.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Kairata Parva (the fight with the Kirata; the empty quivers; Gandiva taken; Arjuna overpowered; worship with a garland; recognition of Shiva)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: the inexhaustible quivers emptied, the bow snatched, the sword breaking on the Kirata's head, the wrestling, Arjuna falling senseless.
Confirm the garland episode: Arjuna makes an earthen altar or image of Shiva, offers a garland, and sees it on the Kirata's head.
The quivers described as never running out follow the epic's description of Arjuna's inexhaustible quivers; confirm.

Editor: 'the flowers he gave to God' changed to 'offered to Shiva' so the narrator speaks from inside the story; 'because of how he fought and how he turned' (narrator's reason) replaced with Shiva's praise of his courage, to confirm in Ganguli.
